The surveys are the evidence of that day; sections 0, 2 and 7 describe the tree as it stands, section 6 the development loop, and the order of work and the open decisions are in coordinator/PLAN.md, to which sections 4 and 5 point. Every claim cites a survey section, a file:line, a commit, or a FACTS or POSITIONS entry. Read after FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md; it does not repeat them. -->

# The territory map

## 0. Terms used here

Path: one of the two execution routes, the interpreter (`fortress <file>.fss`, "walk") or the compiler (`fortress compile` then `fortress run`); "both paths" means the shared front end.

World: which prelude a run links against; the interpreter world is `FortressLibrary` + `FortressBuiltin` + `AnyType`, the compiler world is `CompilerLibrary` + `CompilerBuiltin` + `CompilerAlgebra` + `AnyType` (`compiler/WellKnownNames.java:114-139`, `CompilerAlgebra` since `1bd8d3ad1`; `modules-and-phases.md` B.13).

------
Of the eight mechanisms of `spec-to-implementation.md` §4.1, the compiled path has `nat` and `int` static parameters (the checker since climb batch 4 rung N, `3f297441c`; the run time since batch 5 rung Z, `e893a3e00`), inferring a `bool`, `dim` or `unit` one refused by name; walk has coercion since batch 4 rung C (`b628871a2`); where clauses remain the gap: a where-clause variable in an `extends` clause is undefined on both paths, and codegen refuses any declaration carrying a where clause (`CodeGen.java:2953, :4093, :5004`) (FACTS § Execution model, § The checker and the one library, § Landed semantics).

The gate is strong where the 2012 team spent its last two years (codegen, the compiler front end, diagnostics) and blind where the team stopped: the bytecode optimizer (zero tests), syntax abstraction (one file), the cache round trip (not asserted), the linker, the unparser (`test-coverage.md` C.3); concurrency is seen only by the thirteen compiled `atomic` programs at four threads, since every suite runs one thread (`build.xml:947`, `:1188`).

Contravariance in overloaded dispatch is switched off on every compiled program by a property that defaults true (`fortress.disable.contravariance`, `ProjectProperties.java:327-328`), the 2012 retreat of commit `c35aac139` still in force (`dormant-code.md` §2.2).

The team's rationale in the specification exists only in the draft build (230 `\note{}` boxes and the Internal Document appendix, suppressed by `\ifrelease`), and its deepest layer, 27 named email threads, is not in the repository (`design-intent-sources.md` header, §4); the revival's own changes print in every build (§7, `Specification/`).

## 3. Answers to the questions Pavol asked on 2026-09-16

Is there a small core? The spec's own answer is no: the Internal Document's FAQ calls the core library "fictitious" and defines the language by Core versus Standard library, a split the tree does not have (`design-intent-sources.md` §4, `appendices/FAQ.tex:121-131`). What functions as the core is the mechanism layer of `spec-to-implementation.md` §4.1: traits with multiple inheritance, generics, static parameters of five kinds, operator declarations in traits, multiple dispatch, juxtaposition, coercion, where clauses. Everything numeric is library on top of that.

Is the test suite shared between interpreter and compiler? No. Two hand-ported corpora: `tests/` shares no file name with `compiler_tests/`, and the 11 names it shares with `other_compiler_tests/` are different programs; only `parser_tests/` is read by both suites, and the gate's ladder stage also compiles and runs 82 files of `tests/`, each compared with its own earlier compiled output; nothing compares the two paths on one program (`test-coverage.md` B; FACTS § The harness and the gate).

Where is bytecode generated? `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java` (6,857 lines) writes one jar per component into `bytecode_cache` with ASM; `OverloadSet` generates dispatch methods; `NamingCzar` lowers types; generic instantiation happens later, at load time (`modules-and-phases.md` B.9, B.11).

Where does the grammar extension happen? `syntax_abstractions/`, in two moments: template bodies of a grammar api are parsed when the api is analysed (GRAMMAR phase), and a component that imports the grammar gets a generated parser and is expanded by `Transform` before any phase runs on it (B.3).

Is there Java interop? Yes, two mechanisms that share nothing: `builtinPrimitive("class")` in the interpreter world (368 bindings) and `import java …` in the compiler world (20 lines, `nativeHelpers/` + `nativeInterface/`); `import java` is also wired on the interpreter path by a third route, which does not work and which no test exercises (FACTS § The territory map); Java cannot call Fortress except through `MainWrapper` (B.12).

Where are Fortify and Fortick, and when would we touch them? `Fortify/fortify.el` (8,024 lines) plus `fortify.sty`, driven by `bin/fortify` and an Ant task; `bin/fortick` wraps it for backtick-delimited snippets in a document; `contrib/Emacs/fortress-mode.el` is an ordinary editing mode. They are presentation only; nothing on either path depends on them (A.6, `design-intent-sources.md` §6, the notation row). The Unicode operators and juxtaposition are the language itself; Fortify only typesets them.

Which spec counts? `Specification/`, "Working Draft, July 19, 2012", revision 4267. The sources under `Specification-1.0-frozen/` are byte for byte the team's Working Draft of February 2011, the text `Specification/` held until the revival's revisions, and only the PDF beside them is the 1.0 artefact (FACTS "`Specification-1.0-frozen/` is byte for byte the working draft of 2011-02-02"; `spec-to-implementation.md` §1.2). This corrects the FACTS entry that called the frozen tree "1.0".

## 4. Decisions the surveys put on the table

Every open decision, the surveys' among them, is held in `coordinator/PLAN.md`, in the order it needs deciding ("Pavol's answers, in the order they are needed") or parked ("Off the path, parked"), and each survey's own "Decisions not made" section keeps its original list.

## 5. The gaps on the path, in dependency order

The path in order is `coordinator/PLAN.md`: its six phases run from the climb batches through the checker at a true zero and the switch-over to microGPT compiled and then fast, and its last section says what that order replaced, this section among it.

## 6. The development loop

Measured (`test-coverage.md` D): `ant compileAll` about 80 s and it wipes the interpreter cache through `cleanCache`; `ant testFast` 5 min 23 s with the wall set by the indivisible `othercompiler` track; `ant testSystem` about 2 min in four shards; `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=X` 1 min 26 s for a one-second test, the cost being ant's fileset scan of `build/`; the 280 child JVMs of the `run` tests, at about 200 ms each, are not removable; every grammar-importing run leaves a 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory (`RatsUtil.java:138-144`), swept by `experiment/env.sh`.

The two suites are therefore about nine minutes after a rebuild, before the gate's other stages, and neither test target compiles, so a stale `build/` silently tests the previous revision.

Three loops, fastest first, are what the path needs.

The shadow loop: compile one edited file with scalac or javac against the build classpath and put it first on the classpath; seconds instead of 80 s, no rebuild, no cache wipe, no tracked change. The template prototype ran its whole matrix this way; the recipe is in `perf-probes/template-check/run-all.sh` and `matrix.sh`. This is the loop for checker and code-generator edits.

The program loop: a differential check that runs the three kernels and C4 on both paths and compares output, from `explorations/`; minutes. It is not built, since nothing microGPT-shaped compiles before the switch-over; it is the loop for phases 5 and 6 of `coordinator/PLAN.md`, and the only check that would say whether the target program still works.

The gate loop: the gate of §0, run once on a batch's merged tree before any commit under the sealed tree lands on `main` (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`). Running one JUnit class directly with `junit.textui.TestRunner` and the `fastTrack` macro's properties avoids the 86 s ant tax (the template worker's recipe, `perf-probes/template-check/`).

=== quote
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== trail
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

Yes, it makes sense. Here is what I hear you asking, part by part, then answers to the two direct questions, then how I would produce it.

**What you are asking for.** One document, a map of the territory, written before the sealed tree is opened. It has these parts:

1. **Repository architecture.** The modules in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/` and the top-level directories, each with its role and what it depends on. The repo already has a partial version of this in `explorations/repo-internals.md`; the map either extends it or supersedes it.
2. **Language architecture, spec to implementation.** For each feature area of the latest committed spec (not the 1.0 frozen one), where it lives: in the parser, in the static checker, in the interpreter, in the compiler, in the shipped library, or nowhere. The particular question you named: what enables the numeric tower. The tower is library code, but it stands on traits, generic types, operator overloading and dispatch, and those are language mechanisms implemented in the checker and runtime. The map separates enabling blocks from things built on them.
3. **The compile pipeline, phase by phase.** Rats! parser produces the AST; grammar extensions are expanded; desugaring; type checking; bytecode generation with ASM; the runtime class loader that generates code on the fly; the Java interop surface. For each phase: which module, what it produces, what the next phase needs from it. You are right that there is Java interop, the `nativeHelpers` module and the compiler's `NativeHelper` bindings are that surface.
4. **Test coverage.** Which test directories exercise which layer, whether the interpreter and compiler suites are shared or separate, and how much of each layer has no test at all. This decides how safely each layer can be modified.
5. **Gaps on the path.** Of the 309 ledger rows, which ones sit on the road from today's tree to a fast compiled microgpt, in dependency order, and what breaks if each is left alone.
6. **The development loop.** What makes an iteration slow, which of those costs are ledger rows already, and which are tooling.
7. **A dependency map.** Touching this affects that, so that fixes are ordered and the artifact does not fall apart under edits.

**The guiding constraint you stated.** Finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest spec, not redesign the language. The measuring stick is one program: microgpt compiled to bytecode and running fast. A pure-Java microgpt later gives the floor to aim at.

**The phase boundary you described.** Tag the tree at the unsealing point, then start the next phase: modifying the original sources, with lessons from the explorations. The map is the last prep before that tag.

**Terminology: gate.** A gate is the check a change must pass before it is accepted. Ours has been the fully green suite: `ant testFast` plus `ant testSystem`. The map's coverage part tells us where that gate is blind.

**Fortify and Fortick, answered.** Fortify is an Emacs Lisp program, `Fortify/fortify.el`, 8,024 lines, plus a LaTeX style file. It rewrites Fortress source into LaTeX commands so the spec and papers show code as typeset math. It runs from `bin/fortify` or an Ant task. Fortick is a wrapper script that takes a document with backtick-delimited Fortress snippets and replaces them with the fortified form. Neither touches the language, parser, or runtime. The separate `contrib/Emacs/fortress-mode.el` is an ordinary editing mode. We would touch Fortify only if we changed the spec's LaTeX build or wanted the microgpt article typeset that way. Given your verdict on the notation, that is a no. Your verdict itself I record as a position: the 2D rendering is presentation, not language, and not on our path.

**One correction to your picture.** The Unicode operators and mathematical spelling are in the language itself. Fortress source can be written with `∑`, `∈`, `×` and juxtaposition directly, and the ASCII spellings are aliases the parser accepts. Fortify only adds the typesetting on top. So dropping Fortify loses nothing on our path.

**How I would produce the map.** Survey work goes to Opus workers, one brief per part where it needs reading of code or counting of tests: the module and phase walk (parts 1 and 3), the spec-to-implementation table (part 2), and the test coverage census (part 4). Parts 5 to 7 are design and stay in this thread, built on the ledger and the three survey reports. The map lives in `explorations/coordinator/` beside FACTS and POSITIONS, since it is the thing read at every session start from the next phase on.

Yes, it makes sense. Here is what I hear you asking, part by part, then answers to the two direct questions, then how I would produce it.

**What you are asking for.** One document, a map of the territory, written before the sealed tree is opened. It has these parts:

1. **Repository architecture.** The modules in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/` and the top-level directories, each with its role and what it depends on. The repo already has a partial version of this in `explorations/repo-internals.md`; the map either extends it or supersedes it.
2. **Language architecture, spec to implementation.** For each feature area of the latest committed spec (not the 1.0 frozen one), where it lives: in the parser, in the static checker, in the interpreter, in the compiler, in the shipped library, or nowhere. The particular question you named: what enables the numeric tower. The tower is library code, but it stands on traits, generic types, operator overloading and dispatch, and those are language mechanisms implemented in the checker and runtime. The map separates enabling blocks from things built on them.
3. **The compile pipeline, phase by phase.** Rats! parser produces the AST; grammar extensions are expanded; desugaring; type checking; bytecode generation with ASM; the runtime class loader that generates code on the fly; the Java interop surface. For each phase: which module, what it produces, what the next phase needs from it. You are right that there is Java interop, the `nativeHelpers` module and the compiler's `NativeHelper` bindings are that surface.
4. **Test coverage.** Which test directories exercise which layer, whether the interpreter and compiler suites are shared or separate, and how much of each layer has no test at all. This decides how safely each layer can be modified.
5. **Gaps on the path.** Of the 309 ledger rows, which ones sit on the road from today's tree to a fast compiled microgpt, in dependency order, and what breaks if each is left alone.
6. **The development loop.** What makes an iteration slow, which of those costs are ledger rows already, and which are tooling.
7. **A dependency map.** Touching this affects that, so that fixes are ordered and the artifact does not fall apart under edits.

**The guiding constraint you stated.** Finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest spec, not redesign the language. The measuring stick is one program: microgpt compiled to bytecode and running fast. A pure-Java microgpt later gives the floor to aim at.

**The phase boundary you described.** Tag the tree at the unsealing point, then start the next phase: modifying the original sources, with lessons from the explorations. The map is the last prep before that tag.

**Terminology: gate.** A gate is the check a change must pass before it is accepted. Ours has been the fully green suite: `ant testFast` plus `ant testSystem`. The map's coverage part tells us where that gate is blind.

**Fortify and Fortick, answered.** Fortify is an Emacs Lisp program, `Fortify/fortify.el`, 8,024 lines, plus a LaTeX style file. It rewrites Fortress source into LaTeX commands so the spec and papers show code as typeset math. It runs from `bin/fortify` or an Ant task. Fortick is a wrapper script that takes a document with backtick-delimited Fortress snippets and replaces them with the fortified form. Neither touches the language, parser, or runtime. The separate `contrib/Emacs/fortress-mode.el` is an ordinary editing mode. We would touch Fortify only if we changed the spec's LaTeX build or wanted the microgpt article typeset that way. Given your verdict on the notation, that is a no. Your verdict itself I record as a position: the 2D rendering is presentation, not language, and not on our path.

**One correction to your picture.** The Unicode operators and mathematical spelling are in the language itself. Fortress source can be written with `∑`, `∈`, `×` and juxtaposition directly, and the ASCII spellings are aliases the parser accepts. Fortify only adds the typesetting on top. So dropping Fortify loses nothing on our path.

**How I would produce the map.** Survey work goes to Opus workers, one brief per part where it needs reading of code or counting of tests: the module and phase walk (parts 1 and 3), the spec-to-implementation table (part 2), and the test coverage census (part 4). Parts 5 to 7 are design and stay in this thread, built on the ledger and the three survey reports. The map lives in `explorations/coordinator/` beside FACTS and POSITIONS, since it is the thing read at every session start from the next phase on.

On your word, the three survey workers start.

content.content:
- P-26 **The type group's late positions outweigh the specification's early text where they conflict.** The early text was a wish. The type group then made the language run, for performance and with specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. So their later word wins: the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiler prelude's tower flattened in 2009 and 2010 (P-43), Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper. The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.
- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Next is the algebraic layer: `Ring`, `Field` and what the matrices and tensors of machine learning need, so that the library's traits reach them. It goes into the standard library itself (P-27), not into a tree of the revival's own.
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is hundreds of times slower than Python's interpreter. So no performance decision of any kind, and no edit of C4, the flat model program, for speed, until microGPT runs compiled. The gate never runs the two microGPT programs, too long-running to be tests: it compiles them and records the phase that each reaches. A run of them, once possible, goes to a stage that does not gate.
- P-30 **The microGPT walk check after a batch runs in under a minute.** It runs about two forward-and-backward passes against the reference values, which shows that the model's mathematics still works and that the library's changes did not break it. The full check programs run only when asked. A slower check is to him a waste of time.
- P-32 **The territory map (`coordinator/map/`) maps the tree down to where the design intent is written, in the papers as well as the specification.** It exists so that nothing on record is found again from scratch.
- P-33 **The plan (`coordinator/PLAN.md`) has six phases, approved with their workers.** Phases 1 and 2 are landed: the wrapping operators, the revised specification, the run-time sizes, the flat number tower and the overflow natives. 3 is the checker at a true zero; 4, the switch-over, natives then names; 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's holes; 6, microGPT fast. Where the work stands: PLAN's "Where we stand". Re-approval row 41 (ledger row 320: a component named apart from its api does not link) joins the switch-over's design.

# Where the design intent is written down

The specification says what the language is, not why; the why sits in five places, and this file says which place holds which area.

The five places: `Papers/` (five in-repo paper directories, four of them buildable); the Guy Steele corpus indexed by `research/README.md` (links, plus per-session local copies under the gitignored `research/decks/`); `research/extracts/` (our committed working notes on those sources); the specification's own draft-only apparatus (the `\note{}` boxes and the Internal Document appendix, both suppressed in release builds); and the source tree itself (tool docs, long design comments, aspirational test directories, commit messages).

Two structural facts to carry into the rest of this file.

The rationale that is in the specification is in the *draft* build only: `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex:24-37` defines `\note` as empty when `\release` is set, and `Specification/appendices/appendices.tex:24-26` includes the Internal Document chapter only in the non-release build; "Internal Document" appears 0 times in the text of the published `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf` and twice in the in-repo draft render `Specification/fortress.pdf` (599 pages), which also carries 36 occurrences of the editorial "Victor:" notes that the 1.0 PDF has none of.

The deepest layer of the design record is *not* in the repository: 27 `\note{}` passages point at Sun-internal email threads by subject and date (`grep -rn 'email titled' Specification --include='*.tex'`, e.g. `Specification/appendices/future.tex:65`, `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:28`, `Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex:17`), and `research/README.md:103-105` records that no archive of the project mailing lists was found anywhere as of 2026-08-21.

The documents exist. Two of them, in this order:

1. **The territory map**, `explorations/coordinator/map/README.md`, written on the sixteenth at your request, with its part two `map/modules-and-phases.md`: both pipelines phase by phase, the cache, the runtime, the native interop, and the one table where the two paths diverge.
2. **`explorations/repo-internals.md`**, the older living notes, whose section on the two execution paths is the shorter read.

For `nat` specifically there is `explorations/reviews/nat-checking-plan.md`, the plan that was written and never reviewed, and today's array review judged it.

Your mental model is right up to the class loader, so here is that last piece in plain words. Parsing gives the syntax tree. Names are resolved. On the compile path the checker, in Scala, walks the tree, works out a type for every expression and writes it onto the tree, refusing what breaks the rules. Desugaring rewrites some constructs into simpler ones. The code generator walks the typed tree and writes class files into a cache. Then `fortress run` starts a second JVM with that cache on its class path. The class loader's trick is for generics: a generic trait is compiled once, to a template class with placeholders for its type parameters, and the first time the program needs a specific instance, say a box of doubles, the loader takes the template's bytecode and rewrites it on the spot to that instance. No compiler runs at run time; it is a search-and-replace over bytecode, done by the same bytecode library the compiler uses. Sizes are the open question there: today the loader stamps type names and nothing else, and a size in a type dies at load time with a missing class.

What "teaching the checker `nat`" entails, at the level you need: the checker represents every static argument as a type. A size is not a type, so three things do not exist: a representation for a size, the rule for when two sizes are equal, and inference of a size from a value's shape. Today any two sizes compare equal, so nothing is checked. The theory is old and known, not research: index types with natural-number constraints, Xi and Pfenning's Dependent ML from 1999, and its descendants in Haskell's type-level naturals and X10's constrained types, X10 being Fortress's sibling in the same DARPA programme. The work is implementation in the Scala checker, and the plan already names the files.

The map does not have a page written for exactly this reading, so an Opus worker is writing one now: the compile path from source to running bytecode, one page per stage, what the checker does today and how mature it is, what `nat` needs from it, and the precedents. It lands as a new part of the map, and we read it together.
